prose.summary: A paralegal builds the file the lawyer argues from: pulling contracts apart clause by clause, running the legal research that becomes a brief's footnotes, and keeping a litigation matter organized enough that nothing gets missed at deposition. The line people blur is with legal secretary or admin: this job is measured on the substance of the work product, not on managing someone's calendar, even though scheduling still shows up in a chunk of these postings.
prose.day_to_day: Most weeks split unevenly toward solo desk work, maybe four days heads-down against one day of calls, client intake, or sitting in on a deposition prep session. You open contracts (69% of postings name this outright) and mark up terms, redlines, and obligations before they go back to an attorney for review. There's a research thread running underneath most weeks too: Westlaw searches, case law pulls, memos that summarize what a judge has already ruled on something similar. Litigation support means building and maintaining the file itself, exhibit lists, discovery logs, the spreadsheet that tracks which documents have been produced to opposing counsel. The moment people mention looking forward to is the trial prep crunch, oddly enough: the week before a filing deadline when the whole team is in one room and the case finally has a shape. Fridays tend to be lighter, catching up on case management software and closing out the smaller items that piled up.
prose.work_environment: This is office work, mostly, sitting at a desk with two monitors, one for the document, one for research or email. Only about a quarter of postings offer remote work, and that tracks: client files, especially in litigation, often need to stay inside a firm's document management system, and depositions or court filings pull you into physical rooms. Hours run standard business hours until they don't. A trial date or a closing on a deal will compress two weeks of review into four days, and you're staying late. Outside of those peaks the pace is steady rather than frantic, with the stress coming from deadlines that are set by courts or opposing counsel, not by you.
prose.getting_in: Most postings (41%) require a degree, though it doesn't have to be a paralegal-specific one; a bachelor's in almost anything, paired with a paralegal certificate program (these typically run 4 to 12 months), covers most requirements. A meaningful slice, 4%, waive the degree outright when a candidate has direct litigation or contract experience instead. The median experience asked for is just one year, which means the real bottleneck isn't credentialing, it's landing that first job that gives you a matter to point to. People stall at exactly that point: certificate in hand, no firm willing to be the first one to take a chance. Internships or a stint as a legal assistant during the certificate program are what usually break that stall.
prose.ladder: The shift up is from executing tasks assigned by an attorney to owning a piece of a matter end to end: you're the one who knows where every document in a case lives, not just the one who filed it. A senior paralegal often runs point on discovery for an entire litigation, coordinating with vendors and junior paralegals rather than doing every task by hand. The fork shows up around year four or five: some move into paralegal management, overseeing a team and standardizing how a firm handles intake and case files, while others go deep into a practice area (M&A due diligence, patent litigation) and stay hands-on because that's where the interesting work is. A smaller group uses the experience as a runway toward law school.
prose.suits: People who like this work tend to like precision for its own sake: catching that a contract's indemnification clause contradicts a term three pages earlier, or noticing a date discrepancy in a discovery log that would have sunk a filing. It suits someone who doesn't need to be the one arguing the case to feel invested in whether it goes well. The people who leave are usually the ones who wanted advocacy, not preparation. They took the job assuming it was a step toward being in the room making arguments, and found instead that the room is where you hand someone else the folder.
prose.misconceptions: Outsiders assume the job is mostly typing and filing, when the actual weight of it is judgment: knowing which clause matters, which precedent is on point, which exhibit will get challenged. Another common assumption is that it's a holding pattern for people who couldn't get into law school; plenty of paralegals stay in the role for a full career because they prefer building the case to arguing it, and the pay ceiling ($85k at the 75th percentile) reflects a real, standalone profession rather than a waypoint.
prose.who_qualifies: Lawyers moving laterally are the strongest fit measured here, at a 70% match, since the research, contract, and litigation-support skills transfer almost completely, minus the credential to argue in court. Clinical research coordinators show up too, at 12%, which tracks: both jobs live inside documentation-heavy processes with strict version control and compliance deadlines, though the coordinator would need to build legal-research fluency from scratch.
prose.what_the_numbers_miss: The postings can't show you what a firm's culture does to the job: some practices hand paralegals real ownership of a matter, others keep them doing document review indefinitely. They also can't capture how much the work varies by practice area, corporate transactional work and criminal litigation use the same job title but almost nothing else in common day to day.

steps.do: Get a bachelor's degree in any field
steps.how: Most firms treat this as a baseline regardless of major; English, history, and business are common but not required. This is a 4-year step for most people and the one that can't be shortcut if you're starting from nothing.

These run 4 to 12 months depending on whether you go full-time or evenings, and should include coursework in legal research and litigation support specifically, since those show up in 44% and 36% of postings respectively. Look for an ABA-approved program if you want it to carry weight with larger firms.

steps.do: Learn Westlaw and a case management system
steps.how: Westlaw shows up in 11% of postings by name, but functional fluency in legal research databases generally is assumed everywhere. Most certificate programs include training access; if yours doesn't, ask a local firm about a free trial or take a weekend workshop before applying.

steps.do: Take an internship or legal assistant role
steps.how: This is the step that breaks the experience-without-experience problem, since the median job asks for just one year. Six months to a year in an assistant or intern seat, even unpaid or part-time, gives you a real matter to describe in an interview.

steps.do: Apply directly to litigation and contract-heavy teams
steps.how: Target postings that name contracts and litigation-support explicitly, since those are the two most common skill asks (69% and 36%). You'll know you're ready when you can walk through how you'd organize a discovery log or redline a service agreement without looking it up.

prose.tools: Contract review and Westlaw are the real gatekeepers: if you can't speak to how you'd mark up an indemnification clause or run a targeted case-law search, you won't clear a first interview. Case management software and Excel are close behind, used constantly for tracking deadlines, exhibits, and billing codes. Excel in particular gets used more than people expect, mostly for discovery tracking and timeline building rather than anything financial. The tooling is drifting toward integrated case-management platforms that fold research, document review, and scheduling into one system, so fluency in one of those (rather than isolated tools) is becoming the more useful skill to list.

industries.name: Litigation firms
industries.note: The work centers on discovery, depositions, and trial prep; deadlines are set by courts, so the pace has hard, external triggers.

industries.name: Corporate/transactional firms
industries.note: Mostly contract review and due diligence for deals; quieter day to day but with sharp spikes around closings.

industries.name: In-house legal departments
industries.note: Fewer, broader matters per person, more contract and procurement work, less litigation exposure.

industries.name: Government agencies
industries.note: Often involves criminal investigation support and public records work, with more rigid procedure and slower pace than private practice.

specializations.name: Litigation support technology
specializations.why: E-discovery volumes keep growing, and paralegals who can run the review platforms (not just track documents by hand) are getting pulled into larger, more technical matters.

specializations.name: Contract lifecycle management
specializations.why: Companies moving contract review into SaaS platforms need paralegals who can manage the software as well as the language, and this is where corporate legal departments are actively hiring.

specializations.name: Patent and IP litigation support
specializations.why: The subject matter expertise required (technical documents, prior art searches) makes these paralegals hard to replace and commands a premium within firms that handle IP.

pros: There's a real, visible artifact at the end of most weeks: a filed brief, a closed contract, a discovery log that holds up under scrutiny.
The one-year median experience bar means you can be doing substantive legal work well before most professions let you touch anything that matters.
Trial prep weeks, while exhausting, give you a version of the case's whole shape that few other roles on the team get to see.
The skill set (contract review, legal research) transfers cleanly across practice areas, so getting bored in litigation doesn't mean starting over in corporate.
cons: The deadlines are set by courts and opposing counsel, not by your team, so a filing date can turn a calm week into a late one with no warning.
Remote work is genuinely limited here (25% of postings) because a lot of the file has to stay inside a firm's physical or secured systems.
You do the research and the drafting, but the attorney argues the motion; if you want to be the voice in the room, this role won't get you there without law school.
Contract review, done for years, becomes repetitive in a way that isn't obvious from the outside; the hundredth NDA reads a lot like the first.

faq.q: how long does it take to become a paralegal
faq.a: With a bachelor's degree already in hand, a paralegal certificate program adds 4 to 12 months, and most people land their first role within a few months after that if they've done an internship. Starting from scratch (degree included) the realistic timeline is closer to 4 to 5 years.

faq.q: can you become a paralegal without a law degree
faq.a: Yes, and in fact a law degree isn't required or even common for this role; a paralegal certificate alongside any bachelor's degree is the standard path. About 4% of postings waive the degree entirely for candidates with direct litigation or contract experience.

faq.q: paralegal vs legal secretary, what's the difference
faq.a: A paralegal does substantive legal work (contract review, legal research, litigation support) while a legal secretary handles administrative support like scheduling and correspondence. The postings reflect this split: scheduling shows up in only 14% of paralegal listings, while contracts and research dominate at 69% and 44%.

Sometimes, but it's the exception rather than the norm, with only 25% of postings offering remote work. Document security requirements and the need to be physically present for depositions or filings keep most of this work in an office.

faq.q: how much does a paralegal make
faq.a: The middle of the market sits at $69k, with the lower quarter around $57k and the top quarter at $85k. Where you land in that range depends heavily on practice area and firm size, with corporate and IP work generally paying toward the top.
